name: Ron Fedkiw

current_direction_basis: Driven by the five 2025-2026 items I actually fetched: (1) the arXiv abstract for 'Detangled' (arXiv:2607.09811, submitted 10 Jul 2026), which describes a five-dimensional hair-texture parameter space and 'a generative artificial intelligence approach supervised by a separate neural network trained to label candidate strands'; (2) 'Improving Facial Rig Semantics for Tracking and Retargeting', Computer Graphics Forum e70417 (2026), listed first under the 'Faces - Simulation/Vision/Learning' heading on his own homepage and confirmed via OpenAlex DOI 10.1111/cgf.70417; (3) 'On devising more competitive strategies for creating and avoiding collisions along differentiable trajectories', J. Comp. Phys. (OpenAlex publication date 2025-10-15, printed as vol. 545 #114451 (2026) on his homepage); (4) 'Software-based automatic differentiation is flawed', J. Comp. Phys. 114319 (OpenAlex publication date 2025-09-02); (5) 'Sparse-View 3D Reconstruction of Clothed Humans via Normal Maps', WACV 2025, plus the Computer Graphics Forum 2026 reissue of 'Skinning a Parameterization of Three-Dimensional Space for Neural Network Cloth' (DOI 10.1111/cgf.70556). His homepage bio also states he 'is currently working at the interface between physical simulation and machine learning - having joined the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (SAIL) in 2017', and tags newer work with the keywords 'NEURAL NETWORKS, OPTIMIZATION, DATA DRIVEN'. NOT based on his Stanford Profiles publication list, which is stale and stops at 2013.

evidence.title: Detangled: A Framework for Creating, Editing, and Inferencing Feature Rich Hair Strands
evidence.summary: arXiv abs page fetched: submitted 10 Jul 2026; authors Sarah Jobalia, Yitong Deng, Carolyn Smith, Ronald Fedkiw (Jobalia and Deng are both listed as current Ph.D. students on physbam.stanford.edu). Abstract proposes a five-dimensional parameter space for hair strand texture, separates strand texture from overall style via centerline geometry, and generates new strands 'via a generative artificial intelligence approach supervised by a separate neural network trained to label candidate strands according to our five-parameter description.' Most recent item found for this group.

evidence.title: CS 148 Introduction to Computer Graphics and Imaging (Aut) and CS 205L Continuous Mathematical Methods with an Emphasis on Machine Learning (Win), 2025-26
evidence.summary: Stanford Profiles lists under '2025-26 Courses': 'Continuous Mathematical Methods with an Emphasis on Machine Learning CS 205L (Win)' and 'Introduction to Computer Graphics and Imaging CS 148 (Aut)'. He has taught the same pair every year listed back to 2022-23. His homepage hosts the CS205L slide deck publicly and describes it as 'A survey of numerical approaches to the continuous mathematics used throughout computer science with an emphasis on machine and deep learning.' Both are undergraduate-accessible entry points to him.

undergrad_signals.signal: Listed as instructor of record for CS 195 Supervised Undergraduate Research in 2025-26
undergrad_signals.note: Stanford Profiles, under '2025-26 Courses' > 'Independent Studies (17)', lists verbatim: 'Supervised Undergraduate Research CS 195 (Win, Spr)'. This is an administrative course listing, not an advertised opening, but it confirms he is set up to supervise undergraduate research for credit in Winter and Spring.

undergrad_signals.signal: Listed for undergraduate senior-project and independent-work course numbers in 2025-26
undergrad_signals.note: Same '2025-26 Courses' block lists verbatim: 'Senior Project CS 191 (Aut, Win, Spr)', 'Writing Intensive Senior Research Project CS 191W (Aut, Win, Spr)', 'Independent Work CS 199 (Aut, Win, Spr, Sum)', 'Independent Work CS 199P (Aut, Win, Spr, Sum)', and 'Programming Service Project CS 192 (Aut, Win, Spr, Sum)'. CS 191/191W/199 are the standard Stanford CS undergraduate research/senior-project vehicles.

undergrad_signals.signal: Teaches CS 148 (Introduction to Computer Graphics and Imaging), an undergraduate-facing course, every Autumn
undergrad_signals.note: Listed under 2025-26, 2024-25, 2023-24 and 2022-23 Courses. Taking CS 148 in Autumn is the most concrete, currently-scheduled way for an undergraduate to get in front of him. He also posts the CS205L slide deck openly at https://physbam.stanford.edu/.

undergrad_signals.signal: No undergraduate members listed on the group website
undergrad_signals.note: The 'Students' section of physbam.stanford.edu contains exactly three sub-lists: 'Ph.D. Students' (Kevin (Kevli) Li, Sarah Jobalia, Demi Guo, Haodi He, Yitong Deng, Sharon Lee), 'Former Ph.D. Students' (42 named), and 'Former Postdoctoral Scholars' (7 named). There is no undergraduate, master's, or research-assistant category. A case-insensitive grep of the full page HTML for 'undergrad' returned zero hits.

curis.stanford.edu is a JavaScript single-page app that renders no content to curl, and its data endpoint https://curis.stanford.edu/api/projects returns HTTP 401 {"detail":"Authentication credentials were not provided."}. I could neither confirm nor rule out a Fedkiw CURIS project. A student with Stanford SSO should check CURIS directly.

state_rationale: OUTREACH, not OPENING: I found no 'join', 'openings', 'prospective students', or 'we are recruiting' statement anywhere on physbam.stanford.edu (his only group site, a single long HTML page) or on his Stanford Profiles page, and CURIS project data is behind authentication, so nothing meets the bar for OPENING. Not WATCH either: the lab is unambiguously active, with a July 2026 arXiv submission co-authored by two current Ph.D. students, a 2026 Computer Graphics Forum paper, two 2025 Journal of Computational Physics papers, a WACV 2025 paper, and a 2026 journal review. He is also listed for 'Supervised Undergraduate Research CS 195 (Win, Spr)' and 'Senior Project CS 191' in 2025-26, and teaches CS 148 each Autumn, so an undergraduate has both a credit pathway and a course-based introduction. His email fedkiw@cs.stanford.edu is printed directly on his homepage, which makes a cold email straightforward. One caution worth flagging to a student: his homepage carries a long public note naming three recent Ph.D. graduates by name over unfinished publication obligations and stating 'Many faculty require that Ph.D. students have significant first author publications completed before graduating, and I have now changed my policy as well.' That is a real signal about how he runs the group and is worth reading before making contact.
